name: sound_and_rhythm
description: The sonic layer of prose: sound devices, metrical vocabulary for hearing rhythm, prose cadence and clausulae, sentence-length contours, rhythmic and punctuation-driven pacing moves, paragraph rhythm, and the rhythm faults that give a draft away.

sound_devices.name: alliteration
sound_devices.definition: Repetition of the same initial consonant sound across nearby stressed syllables.
sound_devices.example: The fair breeze blew, the white foam flew, the furrow followed free. (Coleridge)
sound_devices.effect: Binds separate words into one perceptual unit and marks the phrase as deliberately made, so the ear treats it as quotable.
sound_devices.caution: More than two linked pairs in a sentence reads as greeting-card copy; heavy alliteration on abstractions is a reliable purple-prose signal.

sound_devices.name: alliterative binomial
sound_devices.definition: A fixed or improvised two-word pair joined by a conjunction whose members alliterate.
sound_devices.example: safe and sound; part and parcel; rack and ruin
sound_devices.effect: Gives a phrase the finality of an idiom, which is why legal and proverbial language is full of them.
sound_devices.caution: The stock pairs are cliches; coin your own or leave them out.

sound_devices.name: consonance
sound_devices.definition: Repetition of consonant sounds in nearby words regardless of position, most often on final consonants.
sound_devices.example: A stroke of luck struck the black rock.
sound_devices.effect: Knits a passage together below the level of conscious notice; less showy than alliteration because the echo is not at the word's front door.

sound_devices.name: assonance
sound_devices.definition: Repetition of vowel sounds in nearby stressed syllables without matching consonants.
sound_devices.example: And all the air a solemn stillness holds. (Gray)
sound_devices.effect: Sustains a single tone color across a clause; long repeated vowels also slow the reading rate.
sound_devices.caution: Repeated vowels plus repeated final consonants stops being assonance and becomes accidental rhyme.

sound_devices.name: sibilance
sound_devices.definition: A concentration of /s/, /z/, /sh/ and /zh/ sounds.
sound_devices.example: The sea slid past the ship's side, silent, ceaseless.
sound_devices.effect: Produces hush, hiss, seduction, or menace depending on context; the softest way to lower a passage's volume.
sound_devices.caution: Read aloud: dense sibilance turns into a snake-hiss or a lisp in audiobook narration.

sound_devices.name: plosive attack
sound_devices.definition: Clustering of stop consonants /p b t d k g/ in stressed positions.
sound_devices.example: He kicked the crate back against the dock.
sound_devices.effect: Percussive, hard-edged, physical; the sound of impact and of decisions being made.

sound_devices.name: fricative texture
sound_devices.definition: Clustering of continuous friction sounds /f v th s sh h/.
sound_devices.example: A soft wash of surf over shale.
sound_devices.effect: Breathy and unbroken; suits weather, cloth, water, and any process that has no discrete events.

sound_devices.name: liquid consonance
sound_devices.definition: Clustering of /l/ and /r/, the consonants that flow without stopping the airstream.
sound_devices.example: The long lull of the river below the mill.
sound_devices.effect: The most reliable ingredient of euphony; makes a line pourable rather than percussive.

sound_devices.name: nasal resonance
sound_devices.definition: Clustering of /m/, /n/ and /ng/.
sound_devices.example: A hum in the morning, coming and coming on.
sound_devices.effect: Hums rather than strikes; a nasal-heavy final word makes a sentence end warm instead of sharp.

sound_devices.name: velar harshness
sound_devices.definition: Concentration of back-of-the-mouth consonants /k/, /g/, and the guttural cluster.
sound_devices.example: The cracked cog caught, kicked, and quit.
sound_devices.effect: Grating and effortful; the standard sound of machinery, choking, and disgust.

sound_devices.name: euphony
sound_devices.definition: Sound arrangement chosen for ease and pleasantness: open vowels, liquids and nasals, few consonant clusters.
sound_devices.example: The evening air was warm along the water.
sound_devices.effect: Lowers reading effort, which readers experience as elegance and as the writer's authority.
sound_devices.caution: Uninterrupted euphony over a page becomes soporific; harshness is what makes smoothness legible.

sound_devices.name: cacophony
sound_devices.definition: Sound arrangement chosen for harshness: consonant clusters, stops, abrupt shifts between vowel qualities.
sound_devices.example: Grit crackled, the axle jerked, the truck bucked its cargo flat.
sound_devices.effect: Enacts difficulty, violence, or disorder in the mouth of the reader, not just in the report.

sound_devices.name: onomatopoeia
sound_devices.definition: A word whose sound imitates the noise it names.
sound_devices.example: buzz, hiss, clang, thud, splash
sound_devices.effect: Collapses the distance between naming and hearing; the fastest sensory shortcut in the language.
sound_devices.caution: Comic-book onomatopoeia in narrative prose (kaboom, thwack) reads as juvenile unless the register is already playful.

sound_devices.name: phonetic mimesis
sound_devices.definition: Sound patterning across a whole clause so that the movement of the mouth enacts the sense, without any single word being imitative.
sound_devices.example: The moan of doves in immemorial elms, and murmuring of innumerable bees. (Tennyson)
sound_devices.effect: The strongest sound effect available in prose, because it works at the length of a breath rather than a word.
sound_devices.caution: Only convincing when the sense is already there; sound cannot rescue a sentence that says nothing.

sound_devices.name: phonestheme
sound_devices.definition: A sub-morphemic sound cluster that carries meaning across an unrelated family of words.
sound_devices.example: gl- for light (glare, gleam, glint); sn- for the nose (sneer, snout, sniff); -ump for dull mass (lump, clump, stump)
sound_devices.effect: Lets a coinage or an unusual word feel already understood; useful in naming and in invented terminology.

sound_devices.name: sound symbolism
sound_devices.definition: Systematic association between phonetic features and semantic scale, chiefly magnitude: high front vowels for small, low back vowels for large.
sound_devices.example: teeny, itsy, slim versus huge, vast, broad
sound_devices.effect: Gives word choice a second channel of meaning; a small thing named with a back vowel feels off even when the denotation is exact.

sound_devices.name: bouba/kiki effect
sound_devices.definition: The near-universal mapping of round, sonorant sounds to rounded shapes and sharp, plosive sounds to angular ones (Kohler).
sound_devices.example: A product called Balumo reads as soft; one called Kritek reads as hard.
sound_devices.effect: Practical for naming characters, companies, and coinages: the sound sets expectations before the definition arrives.

sound_devices.name: ideophone
sound_devices.definition: A vivid word that depicts a sensory scene as a whole — manner, texture, or movement — rather than naming a sound.
sound_devices.example: zigzag, higgledy-piggledy, helter-skelter, plod
sound_devices.effect: Carries manner and attitude in one token, doing the work of an adverb without the adverb.

sound_devices.name: ablaut reduplication
sound_devices.definition: Doubling a word with a fixed vowel change, in English almost always in the order i-a-o.
sound_devices.example: tick-tock, flip-flop, zigzag, mishmash
sound_devices.effect: Sounds inevitable to a native ear; violating the vowel order (tock-tick) sounds broken, which is itself usable for comic effect.

sound_devices.name: rhyming reduplication
sound_devices.definition: Doubling a word with a change of the initial consonant only.
sound_devices.example: helter-skelter, hocus-pocus, razzle-dazzle
sound_devices.effect: Reads as dismissive or festive; almost never neutral, so it colors whatever it labels.
sound_devices.caution: Dismissive by default — it will trivialize a subject you meant to take seriously.

sound_devices.name: internal rhyme
sound_devices.definition: Rhyme between words inside the same sentence or clause rather than at line ends.
sound_devices.example: The pressure of the measure told.
sound_devices.effect: Marks a phrase for memory; standard in slogans, headlines, and aphorism.
sound_devices.caution: In neutral expository prose, unplanned internal rhyme reads as an accident and stops the reader.

sound_devices.name: slant rhyme
sound_devices.definition: Near rhyme in which consonants match but vowels do not, or the stress falls differently (also half rhyme, pararhyme).
sound_devices.example: grained / groaned; hall / hell
sound_devices.effect: Gives the binding force of rhyme without its chiming closure; useful when full rhyme would be too neat.

sound_devices.name: eye rhyme
sound_devices.definition: Words that look as if they rhyme but do not sound alike.
sound_devices.example: love / move; cough / bough
sound_devices.effect: A purely visual echo; matters in prose only as a trap for writers who compose with the eye and never test aloud.

sound_devices.name: homoioteleuton
sound_devices.definition: Repetition of the same ending syllable or suffix across nearby words or phrase-ends.
sound_devices.example: the deployment of the equipment for the containment of the incident
sound_devices.effect: In verse and deliberate rhetoric it chimes; in prose it is usually the audible symptom of nominalization.
sound_devices.caution: A run of -tion or -ment or -ly endings is the single most common unnoticed rhythm fault in expository writing.

sound_devices.name: polyptoton
sound_devices.definition: Repetition of a root word in different grammatical forms, which chimes at the level of sound as well as sense.
sound_devices.example: With eager feeding food doth choke the feeder. (Shakespeare)
sound_devices.effect: Repeats without the flatness of repeating a word verbatim; makes a conceptual link audible.

sound_devices.name: parechesis
sound_devices.definition: Repetition of similar sound sequences across adjacent words without full rhyme or alliteration.
sound_devices.example: a bland brand of blame
sound_devices.effect: Produces a tight, worked surface; heavy in aphorism and in advertising copy.
sound_devices.caution: Sustained parechesis calls attention to the writer rather than the subject.

sound_devices.name: paromoiosis
sound_devices.definition: Parallel clauses whose sounds correspond position by position, not merely their grammar.
sound_devices.example: He came in silence; he went in shame.
sound_devices.effect: Makes two clauses feel like two halves of one object; the sonic counterpart of isocolon.

sound_devices.name: vowel gradation
sound_devices.definition: Deliberate movement through vowel quality across a phrase, typically front-to-back to darken or back-to-front to brighten.
sound_devices.example: It began as a gleam, became a glow, and settled to a dull dark hum.
sound_devices.effect: Changes the emotional temperature of a sentence without changing a single content word.

sound_devices.name: vowel quantity
sound_devices.definition: Exploiting long versus short vowels to control reading speed.
sound_devices.example: Short: he cut it, quick, and hid it. Long: the road wound slowly toward the loaming shore.
sound_devices.effect: Long vowels lengthen the syllable and slow the line; short vowels clip it. The most direct sonic control over pace.

sound_devices.name: consonant cluster density
sound_devices.definition: The number of adjacent consonants the mouth must negotiate per syllable.
sound_devices.example: strengths, twelfths, glimpsed
sound_devices.effect: Dense clusters cost articulation time and effort, so a cluster-heavy sentence feels laborious even when it is short.

sound_devices.name: monosyllabic texture
sound_devices.definition: A run of one-syllable words, usually of Anglo-Saxon origin.
sound_devices.example: that these dead shall not have died in vain (Lincoln)
sound_devices.effect: Plain, weighted, and hard to argue with; each word gets its own beat, so the line lands like a series of blows.

sound_devices.name: polysyllabic texture
sound_devices.definition: A run of long, usually Latinate words.
sound_devices.example: the institutionalization of administrative discretion
sound_devices.effect: Creates distance, formality, and abstraction; a few unstressed syllables between beats speed the line up while making it harder to feel.

sound_devices.name: hiatus
sound_devices.definition: Collision of a vowel at the end of one word with a vowel at the start of the next, forcing a glottal break.
sound_devices.example: the idea of a united area
sound_devices.effect: Introduces an unplanned stumble; usually a fault, occasionally useful to slow a reader deliberately.
sound_devices.caution: Most audible in read-aloud and audiobook work; fix by reordering or inserting a consonant-initial word.

sound_devices.name: elision
sound_devices.definition: Dropping a sound or syllable so the phrase fits the intended rhythm.
sound_devices.example: over becomes o'er; it is becomes it's; the contraction that keeps a clause at four beats
sound_devices.effect: Contractions are the main modern form: they shorten the line, lower the register, and speed the pulse.

sound_devices.name: mis-juncture
sound_devices.definition: Word-boundary ambiguity where the run of sounds can be resegmented into different words.
sound_devices.example: a nice cream / an ice cream; the stuffy nose / the stuff he knows
sound_devices.effect: Comic or confusing; a genuine hazard in text meant to be heard rather than read.

sound_devices.name: cacemphaton
sound_devices.definition: An accidental obscene or absurd sound sequence produced by innocent adjacent words.
sound_devices.example: a fine tuna sandwich read aloud too quickly
sound_devices.effect: Nothing but a hazard; the reason for the read-aloud pass.
sound_devices.caution: Detectable only by ear — spellcheck and prose linters cannot see it.

meter_basics.name: foot
meter_basics.definition: The basic unit of metrical analysis: one stressed syllable plus its attendant unstressed syllables.
meter_basics.example: de-LIGHT is one foot; DE-li-cate is one foot.
meter_basics.effect: Gives a portable vocabulary for describing prose rhythm precisely instead of calling it choppy or flowing.

meter_basics.name: scansion
meter_basics.definition: Marking a passage's stressed and unstressed syllables to see its rhythm.
meter_basics.example: x / x / x / — we HOLD these TRUTHS to BE
meter_basics.effect: The diagnostic move behind every cadence judgment; scan the last six syllables of a paragraph before you decide it is weak.

meter_basics.name: iamb
meter_basics.definition: An unstressed syllable followed by a stressed one (x /).
meter_basics.example: the WORD, a-GAIN, be-LIEVE
meter_basics.effect: The default rhythm of English phrasing; iambic runs feel neutral and forward-leaning, which is why they disappear into prose.

meter_basics.name: trochee
meter_basics.definition: A stressed syllable followed by an unstressed one (/ x).
meter_basics.example: GAR-den, TA-ble, NEV-er
meter_basics.effect: Falling and emphatic at the start of a clause; a trochaic opening word is the cheapest way to put weight on a sentence's first beat.

meter_basics.name: spondee
meter_basics.definition: Two consecutive stressed syllables (/ /).
meter_basics.example: HEART-BREAK, DEAD WEIGHT, WHITE HOT
meter_basics.effect: Slows and thickens the line; a spondee at a sentence's end is the heaviest available close.

meter_basics.name: pyrrhic
meter_basics.definition: Two consecutive unstressed syllables (x x).
meter_basics.example: in the, of a, on the
meter_basics.effect: Rhythmic filler that speeds a passage but adds no weight; a sentence ending in a pyrrhic dribbles away.

meter_basics.name: anapest
meter_basics.definition: Two unstressed syllables followed by a stressed one (x x /).
meter_basics.example: in-ter-VENE, un-der-STOOD, on the ROAD
meter_basics.effect: Galloping and comic in verse; in prose it produces a rising lift into a stressed close.

meter_basics.name: dactyl
meter_basics.definition: A stressed syllable followed by two unstressed ones (/ x x).
meter_basics.example: MER-ri-ly, HAP-pi-ness, TEN-der-ly
meter_basics.effect: Falling and dying away; the standard ingredient of a soft, receding sentence ending.

meter_basics.name: amphibrach
meter_basics.definition: An unstressed, a stressed, and an unstressed syllable (x / x).
meter_basics.example: re-MEM-ber, e-LEC-tion
meter_basics.effect: Self-contained and rounded; a favorite closing shape in medieval prose cadence.

meter_basics.name: cretic
meter_basics.definition: A stressed, an unstressed, and a stressed syllable (/ x /), also amphimacer.
meter_basics.example: COUNT them OUT; HALF a LOAF
meter_basics.effect: The workhorse of classical prose clausulae — it closes firmly without thudding.

meter_basics.name: molossus
meter_basics.definition: Three consecutive stressed syllables (/ / /).
meter_basics.example: COLD HARD CASH; FULL STOP NOW
meter_basics.effect: Maximum weight and maximum slowness; effective once per chapter, ridiculous twice per page.

meter_basics.name: choriamb
meter_basics.definition: A stressed, two unstressed, and a stressed syllable (/ x x /).
meter_basics.example: OVER the HILL; PICK it up FAST
meter_basics.effect: A bracketed unit with stresses at both edges; makes a phrase feel like a closed container.

meter_basics.name: accentual-syllabic meter
meter_basics.definition: The English metrical system, which counts both stresses and total syllables per line.
meter_basics.example: Iambic pentameter: five iambs, ten syllables.
meter_basics.effect: The frame against which English readers hear all rhythm, including prose rhythm they never consciously scan.

meter_basics.name: accentual meter
meter_basics.definition: Meter that counts stresses only and lets unstressed syllables float.
meter_basics.example: Old English alliterative verse: four stresses a line, two of them alliterating.
meter_basics.effect: The closest metrical model to actual English speech, and therefore to well-tuned prose.

meter_basics.name: stress timing
meter_basics.definition: The tendency of English to space stressed syllables at roughly equal intervals, compressing the unstressed syllables between them.
meter_basics.example: 'DOGS chase CATS' and 'the DOGS have been chasing the CATS' both carry two beats and take about the same time to say; the extra syllables are squeezed into the gaps.
meter_basics.effect: Explains why syllable count is a poor proxy for pace and stress count is a good one.

meter_basics.name: ictus
meter_basics.definition: The beat — the stressed position in a foot, where the reader's pulse lands.
meter_basics.example: In we shall FIGHT on the BEACH-es, the ictus falls on FIGHT and BEACH.
meter_basics.effect: Content words should sit on the ictus; when function words take the beats, the sentence sounds mushy.

meter_basics.name: promotion and demotion
meter_basics.definition: The way a normally unstressed syllable gains stress, or a stressed one loses it, to satisfy the surrounding rhythm.
meter_basics.example: In the reading of the will, of takes a beat it would not have in isolation.
meter_basics.effect: Why scansion is contextual, and why a word's dictionary stress is not the last word on how a sentence sounds.

meter_basics.name: metrical substitution
meter_basics.definition: Replacing the expected foot with a different one to break monotony, most often a trochee in the first position.
meter_basics.example: NEVER in the field of human conflict — a trochee opening an otherwise iambic run.
meter_basics.effect: The main way to keep a regular rhythm from turning mechanical; the prose equivalent is a stressed opening word after a run of iambic starts.

meter_basics.name: catalexis
meter_basics.definition: Dropping the final unstressed syllable of a metrical line so it ends on a stress.
meter_basics.example: TY-ger TY-ger BURN-ing BRIGHT — the last foot is a trochee minus its tail.
meter_basics.effect: Produces a clipped, decisive ending; the metrical name for what prose writers do when they cut a trailing word.

meter_basics.name: anacrusis
meter_basics.definition: One or more unstressed syllables before the first full foot — a run-up into the beat.
meter_basics.example: And THEN the whole thing STOPPED.
meter_basics.effect: A short ramp that delays the first stress; too much anacrusis makes a sentence take a long time to start meaning anything.

meter_basics.name: caesura
meter_basics.definition: A strong sense pause inside a line or clause, usually marked by punctuation.
meter_basics.example: To err is human; || to forgive, divine. (Pope)
meter_basics.effect: Divides a long unit into two hearable halves and gives the reader somewhere to breathe mid-sentence.

meter_basics.name: enjambment
meter_basics.definition: Running a syntactic unit past the end of the metrical or visual unit so the break falls mid-phrase.
meter_basics.example: Milton: 'Of Man's first disobedience, and the fruit / Of that forbidden tree, whose mortal taste / Brought death into the world' — each line ends mid-phrase and the sense runs on.
meter_basics.effect: In prose the analogues are the page turn, the section break, and the chapter end used to strand a clause and pull the reader across.

verse_forms_that_teach_prose.name: blank verse
verse_forms_that_teach_prose.example: Of Man's first disobedience, and the fruit... (Milton)
verse_forms_that_teach_prose.effect: The English default for elevated speech; prose that drifts into it acquires unearned grandeur, which is why accidental pentameter is a fault worth hunting.

verse_forms_that_teach_prose.name: heroic couplet
verse_forms_that_teach_prose.definition: Rhymed iambic pentameter in pairs, usually end-stopped.
verse_forms_that_teach_prose.example: True wit is Nature to advantage dressed, / What oft was thought, but ne'er so well expressed. (Pope)
verse_forms_that_teach_prose.effect: The model for the balanced, antithetical aphorism; teaches how a two-part sentence can close with a click.

verse_forms_that_teach_prose.name: ballad meter
verse_forms_that_teach_prose.definition: Alternating four-stress and three-stress lines, rhyming on the short ones.
verse_forms_that_teach_prose.example: Amazing grace, how sweet the sound / that saved a wretch like me.
verse_forms_that_teach_prose.effect: The most memorable rhythm in English; its 4-3 alternation is the ancestor of the long-sentence, short-sentence prose pattern.

verse_forms_that_teach_prose.name: alliterative accentual verse
verse_forms_that_teach_prose.definition: The Old and Middle English line: four stresses, a strong medial pause, and alliteration binding the halves.
verse_forms_that_teach_prose.example: In a somer seson, whan softe was the sonne (Langland)
verse_forms_that_teach_prose.effect: Shows alliteration used structurally rather than decoratively — as the joint between halves, not as ornament sprinkled on top.

verse_forms_that_teach_prose.name: sprung rhythm
verse_forms_that_teach_prose.definition: Hopkins's system: feet counted by stress alone, with any number of unstressed syllables allowed to crowd between beats.
verse_forms_that_teach_prose.example: The world is charged with the grandeur of God.
verse_forms_that_teach_prose.effect: A license for stress-dense prose; useful when you want a clause to feel compressed and overloaded rather than metrical.

verse_forms_that_teach_prose.name: free verse cadence
verse_forms_that_teach_prose.definition: Unmetered verse whose rhythm comes from phrase length, breath, and line placement rather than a repeating foot.
verse_forms_that_teach_prose.effect: The closest verse practice to prose rhythm, and the best training in tuning by phrase rather than by syllable.

verse_forms_that_teach_prose.name: Whitmanic long line
verse_forms_that_teach_prose.definition: A long, syntactically parallel line built from repeated openings and accumulating clauses.
verse_forms_that_teach_prose.example: I celebrate myself, and sing myself, / And what I assume you shall assume...
verse_forms_that_teach_prose.effect: Teaches how anaphora plus accumulation can carry a very long unit without losing the reader.

verse_forms_that_teach_prose.name: Hebrew parallelism
verse_forms_that_teach_prose.definition: The verse principle of the Psalms and the King James Bible: paired cola that restate, extend, or oppose one another rather than rhyming.
verse_forms_that_teach_prose.example: The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork. (KJV)
verse_forms_that_teach_prose.effect: The deep source of English liturgical cadence and of the balanced two-part sentence; rhythm carried entirely by sense-parallelism.

verse_forms_that_teach_prose.name: biblical colon
verse_forms_that_teach_prose.definition: The short breath-unit of KJV prose — typically five to twelve syllables, and-linked to its neighbors.
verse_forms_that_teach_prose.example: And God said, Let there be light: and there was light. (KJV)
verse_forms_that_teach_prose.effect: A model for coordinate, uninflected narration where every clause carries equal weight.

verse_forms_that_teach_prose.name: haiku compression
verse_forms_that_teach_prose.definition: A short-form discipline of image plus turn within a fixed small budget of syllables.
verse_forms_that_teach_prose.example: An old pond / a frog jumps in / the sound of water. (Basho, trans.)
verse_forms_that_teach_prose.effect: Trains the habit of cutting to the two images that matter and letting the juxtaposition do the argument.

verse_forms_that_teach_prose.name: prose poem
verse_forms_that_teach_prose.definition: A composition printed as prose that uses verse's density of sound, image, and cadence without lineation.
verse_forms_that_teach_prose.example: Baudelaire's Petits poemes en prose; Rimbaud's Illuminations.
verse_forms_that_teach_prose.effect: The proof case that rhythm in prose is a designed, not incidental, property.
verse_forms_that_teach_prose.caution: Its permissions do not transfer wholesale — a chapter of exposition written at prose-poem density exhausts readers.

prose_cadence.name: clausula
prose_cadence.definition: The metrical shape of the last few syllables of a prose sentence or colon, treated by ancient rhetoricians as the point where rhythm is heard most.
prose_cadence.example: Cicero's favored close was the cretic plus trochee (/ x / | / x): esse videatur; in English, WHAT it might COST us.
prose_cadence.effect: Readers register a sentence's rhythm chiefly at its end; the clausula is therefore the highest-leverage place to tune.
prose_cadence.caution: A signature clausula repeated sentence after sentence turns prose into chant.

prose_cadence.name: cursus planus
prose_cadence.definition: Medieval Latin cadence with the shape stressed, two unstressed, stressed, unstressed (/ x x / x).
prose_cadence.example: GLO-ri-a NOM-i-nis; ENGlish: SETtled the ARgument
prose_cadence.effect: The plainest and most common of the four cursus forms: firm without being final, good for mid-paragraph sentences.

prose_cadence.name: cursus tardus
prose_cadence.definition: Cadence ending stressed, two unstressed, stressed, two unstressed (/ x x / x x) — a slow, trailing close.
prose_cadence.example: GLO-ri-a MAR-ty-rum; English: CARried it QUIetly
prose_cadence.effect: Retards the ending and softens it; use where you want the paragraph to settle rather than snap shut.

prose_cadence.name: cursus velox
prose_cadence.definition: Cadence with the shape stressed, two unstressed, two unstressed, stressed, unstressed (/ x x x x / x) — the swift close.
prose_cadence.example: GLO-ri-a se-cu-LO-rum; English: CARried the deciSION for us
prose_cadence.effect: Puts a run of light syllables between two stresses so the ending arrives fast and lands lightly.

prose_cadence.name: cursus trispondaicus
prose_cadence.definition: The fourth medieval cadence, stressed, unstressed, two unstressed, stressed, unstressed (/ x x x / x).
prose_cadence.example: GLO-ri-fi-CA-mus te; English: FOLlowed inevitably
prose_cadence.effect: A longer run-up to the final stress; the most Latinate-sounding of the four in English.

prose_cadence.name: double cretic close
prose_cadence.definition: Two cretics in succession (/ x / / x /).
prose_cadence.example: COUNT them OUT, ONE by ONE
prose_cadence.effect: Balanced and hammering; suited to a summary sentence that must sound like a verdict.

prose_cadence.name: ditrochee close
prose_cadence.definition: Two trochees ending a period (/ x / x), also dichoreus.
prose_cadence.example: PAtience, PAtience; NOthing FOLlowed
prose_cadence.effect: A falling, rocking close; the Roman critics thought it too sweet, and it can still sound self-satisfied.
prose_cadence.caution: Ancient objection stands: overused, the ditrochee makes prose sound smug.

prose_cadence.name: masculine ending
prose_cadence.definition: A sentence that ends on a stressed syllable, most emphatically a stressed monosyllable.
prose_cadence.example: It cost him the farm.
prose_cadence.effect: The hardest available stop; nothing follows the beat, so the silence after the period is part of the effect.
prose_cadence.caution: Every sentence ending on a hard monosyllable becomes a drumroll of finality that flattens the ones that matter.

prose_cadence.name: feminine ending
prose_cadence.definition: A sentence that ends on one or more unstressed syllables after the final stress.
prose_cadence.example: It cost him the property.
prose_cadence.effect: Softer and more conversational; the trailing syllables let the reader move on rather than stop.

prose_cadence.name: dying fall
prose_cadence.definition: A closing cadence of falling feet — dactyls or trochees — so the sentence recedes rather than lands.
prose_cadence.example: That strain again! It had a dying fall. (Shakespeare)
prose_cadence.effect: Melancholy, resignation, or gentleness; the standard close for an elegiac paragraph.

prose_cadence.name: rising close
prose_cadence.definition: A closing cadence of rising feet — iambs or anapests — climbing into the final stress.
prose_cadence.example: and no one ever came back at all
prose_cadence.effect: Builds momentum into the last word, so a rising close feels like arrival rather than stop.

prose_cadence.name: terminal monosyllable landing
prose_cadence.definition: Ending a sentence on a short, concrete, one-syllable Anglo-Saxon word.
prose_cadence.example: and then the money was gone
prose_cadence.effect: Maximum thud; makes any assertion sound like a fact settled long ago.
prose_cadence.caution: The most imitable of all cadence tricks and therefore the fastest to become a tic.

prose_cadence.name: prepositional tail
prose_cadence.definition: A sentence that trails off into a stack of prepositional phrases after its real ending.
prose_cadence.example: The committee rejected the plan in a meeting on Thursday in the annex of the building on Third Street.
prose_cadence.effect: Dissipates the close; the reader's attention runs out before the syntax does.
prose_cadence.caution: The commonest weak ending in institutional prose. Cut back to the last stressed content word.

prose_cadence.name: participial tail
prose_cadence.definition: A close that ends in an -ing phrase hanging off the main clause.
prose_cadence.example: She signed the form, hoping it would be enough, wondering if anyone would read it.
prose_cadence.effect: Softens and prolongs; legitimate for a receding close, deadly when every third sentence does it.
prose_cadence.caution: A signature of drafting on autopilot — check the density of sentence-final -ing before revision ends.

prose_cadence.name: stress clash
prose_cadence.definition: Two stressed syllables colliding where the rhythm wants a gap.
prose_cadence.example: the STARK CONtrast SHOWED CLEAR SIGNS
prose_cadence.effect: Slows and roughens; occasionally useful for emphasis, usually just awkward.
prose_cadence.caution: Fix by inserting a light word or reordering, not by cutting content.

prose_cadence.name: stress lapse
prose_cadence.definition: Three or more unstressed syllables in a row, leaving the line without a beat.
prose_cadence.example: in a manner of a similar sort
prose_cadence.effect: Rhythmic vacuum; the sentence goes flabby and the reader's attention drops.
prose_cadence.caution: Usually a symptom of prepositional padding — the cure is deletion.

prose_cadence.name: isocolon rhythm
prose_cadence.definition: Successive clauses of equal or near-equal syllable length.
prose_cadence.example: I came, I saw, I conquered.
prose_cadence.effect: Symmetry the ear can verify; makes a formulation sound tested rather than improvised.
prose_cadence.caution: Beyond three members, exact equality starts to sound like liturgy.

prose_cadence.name: tricolon crescendo
prose_cadence.definition: Three parallel members of increasing length (also ascending tricolon or the law of increasing members).
prose_cadence.example: government of the people, by the people, for the people (Lincoln)
prose_cadence.effect: The most reliable escalating cadence in English; the growth in length is what makes the third member feel like a conclusion.
prose_cadence.caution: Its reliability is the problem — a chapter with a tricolon at every section end reads as machine-tuned.

prose_cadence.name: periodic close
prose_cadence.definition: The resolution point of a periodic sentence, where the delayed main clause finally arrives.
prose_cadence.example: If the reports were true, and if the dates could be trusted, and if anyone had bothered to read them, the audit would have failed.
prose_cadence.effect: All the suspended tension discharges at once; the strongest available cadence for a paragraph's final sentence.
prose_cadence.caution: Requires the reader to hold everything in memory — one per page is generous.

prose_cadence.name: biblical cadence
prose_cadence.definition: Coordinate clauses of similar length linked by and, each carrying equal rhythmic weight.
prose_cadence.example: And the evening and the morning were the first day. (KJV)
prose_cadence.effect: Levels hierarchy: every event gets the same beat, which reads as either sacred or numb depending on the material.
prose_cadence.caution: Instantly recognizable as pastiche when the subject matter is mundane.

prose_cadence.name: loose cadence
prose_cadence.definition: The rhythm of a sentence that reaches its main point early and then adds modifiers, each addition a small settling motion.
prose_cadence.example: He shut the door, quietly, with the flat of his hand, as if the house were asleep.
prose_cadence.effect: Conversational and unspooling; the default rhythm of modern narrative prose.

prose_cadence.name: suspended cadence
prose_cadence.definition: A rhythm that withholds the beat the reader is waiting for by delaying the verb or the object.
prose_cadence.example: The letter, which had crossed two oceans and outlived its sender, arrived.
prose_cadence.effect: Creates tension in the body, not just the mind; the reader is physically waiting to exhale.

prose_cadence.name: read-aloud test
prose_cadence.definition: The practice of speaking a passage at reading pace to locate cadence faults that the eye cannot detect.
prose_cadence.example: Wherever you have to reread a clause to breathe correctly, the rhythm is wrong.
prose_cadence.effect: The only reliable diagnostic for stress clash, hiatus, accidental meter, and trailing closes.
prose_cadence.caution: Subvocalized reading is not the same test — the faults hide until the air moves.

sentence_length_contours.name: crescendo contour
sentence_length_contours.definition: Successive sentences that grow longer through a paragraph.
sentence_length_contours.example: He stopped. He listened at the door for a while. He listened until the sound resolved into two voices, one of them his own name.
sentence_length_contours.effect: Widens the reader's frame as the paragraph proceeds; good for a scene opening out or an argument accumulating conditions.

sentence_length_contours.name: diminuendo contour
sentence_length_contours.definition: Successive sentences that shorten toward the end of a paragraph.
sentence_length_contours.example: A long inventory of everything the audit found, then a shorter sentence, then: None of it mattered.
sentence_length_contours.effect: Narrows to a point; the standard shape for a paragraph that ends in judgment.

sentence_length_contours.name: sawtooth contour
sentence_length_contours.definition: Alternating long and short sentences at a steady beat.
sentence_length_contours.effect: High measured variance with a predictable pattern; energetic on a page, mechanical over three.
sentence_length_contours.caution: Regular alternation is still regularity — vary the amplitude, not just the direction.

sentence_length_contours.name: plateau contour
sentence_length_contours.definition: A run of sentences all near the same length.
sentence_length_contours.effect: Steadies and calms; legitimate for procedural explanation where the reader wants uniform footing.
sentence_length_contours.caution: The single most common quantitative signature of machine-drafted prose. Low variance across a whole chapter reads as flat regardless of content quality.

sentence_length_contours.name: spike contour
sentence_length_contours.definition: One sentence far longer or shorter than everything around it.
sentence_length_contours.example: A paragraph of medium sentences interrupted by a five-word one.
sentence_length_contours.effect: The spike takes the emphasis by contrast alone, without any lexical intensifier.

sentence_length_contours.name: ramp and drop
sentence_length_contours.definition: A steady lengthening followed by an abrupt short sentence.
sentence_length_contours.example: Three sentences that build to forty words, then: It failed.
sentence_length_contours.effect: The workhorse paragraph shape in narrative nonfiction; the drop converts accumulated detail into a verdict.

sentence_length_contours.name: hourglass contour
sentence_length_contours.example: Setup at length, a short pivot sentence, then an expanded consequence.
sentence_length_contours.effect: The short middle sentence works as a hinge the reader can feel; useful when a paragraph turns.

sentence_length_contours.name: staircase ascent
sentence_length_contours.definition: Sentences increasing in length by discrete steps rather than smoothly.
sentence_length_contours.effect: Reads as deliberate gathering — each new plateau feels like a decision to go further.

sentence_length_contours.name: terraced descent
sentence_length_contours.definition: Sentence length dropping in steps with pauses at each level.
sentence_length_contours.effect: Controlled deceleration; less abrupt than ramp-and-drop and better for endings that must feel considered rather than sudden.

sentence_length_contours.name: pendulum contour
sentence_length_contours.definition: Length swinging around a mean with increasing or decreasing amplitude.
sentence_length_contours.effect: The most natural-sounding contour because it mimics speech under rising emotion; widening amplitude reads as escalation.

sentence_length_contours.name: short-burst cluster
sentence_length_contours.definition: Three to six very short sentences grouped together inside longer surroundings.
sentence_length_contours.example: The lights went out. Someone swore. A door slammed. Then nothing.
sentence_length_contours.effect: Compresses time and raises the pulse; the standard prose device for action and panic.
sentence_length_contours.caution: Past about six, the reader stops feeling urgency and starts noticing the technique.

sentence_length_contours.name: long-tail paragraph
sentence_length_contours.definition: A paragraph whose final sentence is markedly the longest.
sentence_length_contours.example: Short observations, then a closing sentence that runs the length of the paragraph's argument.
sentence_length_contours.effect: Ends in expansion rather than closure; useful when the point is that the implications keep going.

sentence_length_contours.name: isometric monotony
sentence_length_contours.definition: Near-identical sentence lengths sustained across paragraphs, with variance measured in a word or two.
sentence_length_contours.example: A chapter whose sentences all fall between 17 and 23 words.
sentence_length_contours.effect: None intended — the reader disengages without being able to say why.
sentence_length_contours.caution: Explicit AI tell. Low burstiness is what prose_metrics.py measures; fix by writing one deliberately very short and one deliberately very long sentence per paragraph.

sentence_length_contours.name: burstiness target
sentence_length_contours.definition: A working range for the variance in sentence length within a passage, expressed as a standard deviation or a max/min ratio.
sentence_length_contours.example: A ratio of at least 5:1 between the longest and shortest sentence in any given paragraph.
sentence_length_contours.effect: Turns rhythm into a checkable property rather than a taste judgment.
sentence_length_contours.caution: A target, not a rule — hitting it by inserting decorative fragments is worse than missing it.

rhythm_moves.name: hammer sentence
rhythm_moves.definition: A very short sentence placed immediately after a long one, taking its emphasis entirely from the contrast.
rhythm_moves.example: For eleven months the committee gathered testimony, commissioned three independent reviews, and drafted a report no one outside the building would ever read. Then the funding stopped.
rhythm_moves.effect: Converts accumulated exposition into consequence; the reader hears a verdict without being told one is coming.
rhythm_moves.caution: The best-known rhythm move in English nonfiction and therefore the most parodied. One per section.

rhythm_moves.name: running start
rhythm_moves.definition: Opening with a subordinate clause or adverbial so the sentence has a ramp before its main stress.
rhythm_moves.example: Because no one had checked the dates, the whole schedule was wrong.
rhythm_moves.effect: Delays the first beat and sets a condition before the claim; used sparingly it varies the attack of a paragraph.
rhythm_moves.caution: Three consecutive sentences opening on a subordinate clause is a rhythm rut a linter can catch.

rhythm_moves.name: delayed verb
rhythm_moves.definition: Holding the main verb back behind intervening material so the sentence stays syntactically unfinished.
rhythm_moves.example: The auditor, who had spent a decade on cases like this one and had learned to distrust round numbers, refused.
rhythm_moves.effect: Keeps the reader's breath held; the verb, when it arrives, takes disproportionate stress.

rhythm_moves.name: cumulative build
rhythm_moves.definition: Stating the main clause first and then adding free modifiers, each one specifying further.
rhythm_moves.example: He walked out, coat open, keys in his fist, not looking back at the house.
rhythm_moves.effect: Feels like perception unfolding in real time; the rhythm of a mind noticing rather than a report summarizing.

rhythm_moves.name: staccato run
rhythm_moves.definition: A sequence of short, end-stopped sentences of similar length.
rhythm_moves.example: He counted. He wrote it down. He counted again.
rhythm_moves.effect: Clipped and pressurized; slows narrative time while speeding reading time.
rhythm_moves.caution: Sustained past a paragraph it reads as hardboiled pastiche.

rhythm_moves.name: breath-length phrasing
rhythm_moves.definition: Building sentences out of units of roughly seven to twelve syllables — the span a reader can say in one comfortable breath.
rhythm_moves.example: He set down the glass, || wiped the ring it left, || and waited.
rhythm_moves.effect: Makes prose speakable, which is the underlying reason well-phrased writing feels easy.

rhythm_moves.name: triadic rhythm
rhythm_moves.definition: Grouping items, clauses, or sentences in threes.
rhythm_moves.example: Cold, tired, and out of arguments.
rhythm_moves.effect: Three is the smallest number that establishes a pattern and completes it in the same gesture.
rhythm_moves.caution: Universal enough to be invisible until it isn't; count your triads per chapter, because drafting LLMs produce them at several times human rates.

rhythm_moves.name: drumbeat close
rhythm_moves.definition: Ending a sentence with consecutive stressed monosyllables.
rhythm_moves.example: It was not close. It was not fair. It was not new.
rhythm_moves.effect: Turns the close into percussion; each word lands separately.

rhythm_moves.name: syncopation
rhythm_moves.definition: Placing a stress where the established rhythm did not expect one, usually by inverting a foot or fronting a word.
rhythm_moves.example: After a run of iambic openings: Gone, all of it, in a week.
rhythm_moves.effect: The rhythmic equivalent of a raised eyebrow; keeps a regular passage from becoming metrical.

rhythm_moves.name: pause before the punch
rhythm_moves.definition: Inserting a comma, dash, or parenthesis immediately before the payoff word.
rhythm_moves.example: The audit found exactly one irregularity — his.
rhythm_moves.effect: The silence does the emphasis; no intensifier can match a well-placed delay.

rhythm_moves.name: em-dash swerve
rhythm_moves.definition: Breaking the sentence's direction mid-course with a dash and a countermovement.
rhythm_moves.example: The plan was sound, well funded, endorsed by everyone who mattered — and abandoned within the year.
rhythm_moves.effect: Enacts a change of mind in the sentence's own shape.
rhythm_moves.caution: Dash density is a measured AI tell; two per page is plenty, and a dash used where a comma would do wastes the move.

rhythm_moves.name: fragment burst
rhythm_moves.definition: A short run of verbless or subjectless fragments.
rhythm_moves.example: No warning. No paperwork. Just the locks changed.
rhythm_moves.effect: Strips syntax to nouns and images; fastest way to raise urgency without exclamation.
rhythm_moves.caution: Fragments only read as deliberate against a background of complete sentences.

rhythm_moves.name: asyndetic acceleration
rhythm_moves.definition: Removing conjunctions from a series so the items run together.
rhythm_moves.example: He packed, paid, left.
rhythm_moves.effect: Speeds the line and implies the list could continue; the standard rhythm of haste.

rhythm_moves.name: polysyndetic drag
rhythm_moves.definition: Adding a conjunction before every item in a series.
rhythm_moves.example: and the dust and the heat and the flies and the waiting
rhythm_moves.effect: Slows the line and makes each item weigh the same; the rhythm of endurance and accumulation.

rhythm_moves.name: list escalation
rhythm_moves.definition: Ordering a series so each member is longer or heavier than the last.
rhythm_moves.example: for a day, for a season, for the rest of a working life
rhythm_moves.effect: The list itself becomes an argument about scale; reversing the order deflates deliberately.

rhythm_moves.name: appositive beat
rhythm_moves.definition: Dropping a renaming phrase between commas so the sentence takes an extra rhythmic step.
rhythm_moves.example: The clerk, a man who had signed nine thousand of these, signed it.
rhythm_moves.effect: Adds information without adding a sentence, and creates a mid-line pause the reader can breathe in.

rhythm_moves.name: absolute-phrase coda
rhythm_moves.definition: Ending a sentence with an absolute construction — a noun plus participle detached from the main clause.
rhythm_moves.example: He stood in the doorway, hat in hand, the rain still coming down behind him.
rhythm_moves.effect: A rhythmic tail that widens the frame after the action is complete; camera pulling back.

rhythm_moves.name: refrain
rhythm_moves.definition: Repeating a phrase at intervals so its recurrence becomes part of the rhythm of a section.
rhythm_moves.example: A chapter that returns three times to: The file was still open.
rhythm_moves.effect: Creates structure the reader feels without being told; each return means more than the last.

rhythm_moves.name: anaphoric pulse
rhythm_moves.definition: Repeating the same opening words across successive sentences or clauses to set a beat.
rhythm_moves.example: We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds... (Churchill)
rhythm_moves.effect: The most propulsive rhythmic device in oratory; the repetition becomes a metronome the content rides on.
rhythm_moves.caution: Written prose tolerates far less of it than speech does — three members, then break the pattern.

rhythm_moves.name: epistrophic close
rhythm_moves.definition: Repeating the same word or phrase at the end of successive units.
rhythm_moves.example: of the people, by the people, for the people (Lincoln)
rhythm_moves.effect: Puts the beat at the point of maximum stress; more emphatic and less breathless than anaphora.

rhythm_moves.name: the turn
rhythm_moves.definition: A rhythmic pivot at a single hinge word — but, still, except, and yet — that reverses the direction of a passage.
rhythm_moves.example: Everything about the proposal was defensible. Except the timing.
rhythm_moves.effect: The prose analogue of the sonnet's volta; the reader feels the argument change gear.

rhythm_moves.name: question beat
rhythm_moves.definition: Interrupting a run of declaratives with a short interrogative.
rhythm_moves.example: Three paragraphs of evidence, then: So who signed it?
rhythm_moves.effect: Changes the intonation contour and re-engages a reader who has settled into passive reception.
rhythm_moves.caution: A rhetorical question that the next sentence immediately answers is a stock filler move; make the question do real work.

rhythm_moves.name: callback beat
rhythm_moves.definition: Reprising an earlier phrase in shortened form at a rhythmically prominent position.
rhythm_moves.example: A chapter that opened on a full description of the locked room closing on: The room, still locked.
rhythm_moves.effect: Gives a section audible closure and rewards the attentive reader with recognition.

rhythm_moves.name: rhythmic reversal
rhythm_moves.definition: Inverting an established length pattern — short-short-long where the reader expects long-long-short.
rhythm_moves.example: After a page of ramp-and-drop paragraphs, one that starts short and ends in a forty-word sentence.
rhythm_moves.effect: Prevents the reader's ear from predicting the page; the cure for a well-tuned but exhausted contour.

rhythm_moves.name: the swell
rhythm_moves.definition: Building rhythm across several sentences toward a paragraph's loudest point rather than within one sentence.
rhythm_moves.example: Successive sentences adding a clause each until the last runs three clauses long.
rhythm_moves.effect: Paragraph-scale crescendo; carries emotional escalation without any adverb of intensity.

rhythm_moves.name: the drop
rhythm_moves.definition: Cutting immediately from a passage's rhythmic peak to something short, flat, and factual.
rhythm_moves.example: After the swell: The meeting adjourned at four.
rhythm_moves.effect: Deflation used as punctuation; the flatness after a peak is what makes the peak audible in retrospect.

pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.name: breath comma
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.definition: A comma placed for phrasing rather than grammar, marking where a speaker would pause.
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.example: And then, nothing.
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.effect: Buys a beat of silence; the cheapest rhythmic control in punctuation.
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.caution: House styles that comma strictly by rule will strip these; know which battle you are in.

pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.name: comma splice for speed
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.definition: Joining independent clauses with commas alone so they run without full stops.
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.example: He ran, he fell, he got up, he kept going.
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.effect: Speeds and links; the clauses read as one continuous event rather than four.
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.caution: Only legible as deliberate in a text whose punctuation is otherwise correct — and copy editors will fix it unless you flag it.

pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.name: comma excision
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.definition: Deleting optional commas so a clause runs unbroken.
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.example: Before: In the morning, after the rain, they left. After: In the morning after the rain they left.
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.effect: Removes the reader's rest stops and raises the pace without changing a word.

pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.name: serial comma beat
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.definition: Using (or omitting) the comma before the final conjunction in a list, which changes the rhythm of the last item.
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.example: red, white, and blue vs. red, white and blue
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.effect: With the serial comma the last item stands alone; without it the last two pair up. A rhythmic choice as much as a clarity one.

pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.name: comma cascade
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.definition: A long asyndetic series of comma-separated elements.
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.example: the ledgers, the invoices, the shipping manifests, the two phones, the safe
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.effect: Accumulation without hierarchy; the reader feels quantity rather than counting it.

pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.name: semicolon hinge
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.definition: A semicolon balancing two independent clauses of comparable weight.
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.example: The rule was clear; the practice was not.
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.effect: A pause longer than a comma and lighter than a period, holding two halves in one gesture.
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.caution: Semicolons raise register. In a colloquial voice they read as a lapse into essay mode.

pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.name: colon as gate
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.definition: A colon announcing that what follows delivers what the first clause promised.
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.example: There was only one problem: nobody had the key.
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.effect: Creates anticipation and then satisfies it in the same sentence; the strongest single-sentence setup-payoff device.

pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.name: dash interruption
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.definition: A single em dash cutting into the sentence to insert a contrary or unexpected element.
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.example: He signed everything they put in front of him — including the receipt for his own dismissal.
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.effect: Reads as an interruption of thought rather than a planned clause, which lends spontaneity.
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.caution: Em-dash frequency is one of the most reliable quantitative AI tells; audit density before release.

pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.name: paired dashes
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.definition: Two dashes bracketing an aside that stays at full volume.
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.example: The deadline — everyone knew this — had never been real.
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.effect: Inserts commentary without lowering it to a whisper the way parentheses do.

pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.name: parenthetical drop
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.definition: Enclosing material in parentheses so it reads at lower volume.
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.example: The vote passed (barely).
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.effect: Creates two levels of loudness in one sentence; the aside sounds like an aside.
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.caution: Long parentheses defeat the purpose — anything the reader must hold for more than a clause should be its own sentence.

pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.name: terminal dash
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.definition: A dash at the end of a sentence marking a cut-off rather than a completion.
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.example: If anyone had bothered to ask —
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.effect: Sound of interruption; standard in dialogue for being cut off, distinct from the ellipsis's fade.

pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.name: ellipsis trail
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.definition: Three points marking a fade rather than a stop.
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.example: He said he would call...
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.effect: Trails the voice off; suggests continuation the writer declines to supply.
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.caution: Reads as coy or lazy in expository prose; almost always better replaced by a full stop or a real clause.

pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.name: full-stop drumbeat
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.definition: Consecutive short sentences ending in periods where commas or conjunctions would be idiomatic.
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.example: It was late. He was tired. He signed.
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.effect: Every period is a rest; the paragraph acquires a percussive pulse.

pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.name: period fragment
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.definition: Punctuating a phrase as a sentence to give it a full stop's worth of pause.
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.example: All of it. Gone.
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.effect: Isolates a phrase at the strongest available level of emphasis.
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.caution: Loses force in proportion to frequency; the second one on a page costs the first one half its value.

pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.name: question mark beat
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.definition: A question's rising intonation used to change the melodic contour of a run of statements.
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.example: The numbers were checked twice. Were they?
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.effect: Introduces doubt as sound before introducing it as content.

pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.name: exclamation spike
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.definition: An exclamation point marking maximum volume.
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.example: Get out!
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.effect: Instantly raises the register; in dialogue it is speech, in narration it is the author shouting.
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.caution: Outside dialogue, exclamation points in adult nonfiction read as amateur. Fitzgerald's line about laughing at your own joke applies.

pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.name: paragraph break as rest
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.definition: The white space between paragraphs functioning as a pause longer than any punctuation mark.
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.example: A one-line paragraph surrounded by white space above and below.
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.effect: The longest silence available without a section break; where you put it determines what the reader dwells on.

pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.name: section break
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.definition: A blank line or ornament between passages, functioning as a movement break.
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.example: A dinkus or extra vertical space between scenes.
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.effect: Signals a jump in time, place, or voice; the reader resets expectations across it.

pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.name: italic stress accent
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.definition: Italicizing a word to force stress onto a syllable the neutral reading would not stress.
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.example: I never said he took the money.
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.effect: Overrides the default intonation contour; the only way to specify spoken emphasis in print.
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.caution: If the sentence needs italics to be understood, the word order is usually wrong. Rewrite before you italicize.

pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.name: over-punctuation choppiness
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.definition: Commas and dashes inserted at every available grammatical seam.
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.example: The report, however, which had, by then, been revised, twice, was, finally, released.
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.effect: The sentence stumbles; the reader gets no run of more than three words.
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.caution: Usually a symptom of an overloaded sentence — split it rather than repunctuating it.

pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.name: colon versus dash
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.definition: The choice between a colon (formal, promissory, expected) and a dash (informal, abrupt, surprising) for the same setup-payoff structure.
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.example: One thing was missing: the signature. / One thing was missing — the signature.
pause_and_punctuation_rhythm.effect: Identical syntax, different register and different speed. The colon says here it comes; the dash says here it is.

paragraph_rhythm.name: downbeat opening
paragraph_rhythm.definition: Beginning a paragraph with a short declarative that carries its main stress on the first content word.
paragraph_rhythm.effect: Marks the top of the paragraph as a beat; makes skim-reading the first sentences a coherent experience.

paragraph_rhythm.name: one-sentence paragraph
paragraph_rhythm.definition: A paragraph consisting of a single sentence, usually short, set off by white space on both sides.
paragraph_rhythm.effect: Maximum isolation and therefore maximum emphasis at paragraph scale.
paragraph_rhythm.caution: In tabloid and blog registers it becomes the default and stops meaning anything; ration it.

paragraph_rhythm.name: paragraph-final stress
paragraph_rhythm.definition: Placing the paragraph's most important element in its last sentence, and that sentence's payload in its last words.
paragraph_rhythm.example: Ending on: and the money had already moved.
paragraph_rhythm.effect: Aligns the two positions readers remember best — the end of the paragraph and the end of the sentence.

paragraph_rhythm.name: tapering paragraph
paragraph_rhythm.definition: A paragraph whose sentences shorten steadily toward the close.
paragraph_rhythm.effect: Deceleration into a landing; the standard shape for a paragraph that ends in judgment or resignation.

paragraph_rhythm.name: building paragraph
paragraph_rhythm.definition: A paragraph whose sentences lengthen toward the close.
paragraph_rhythm.effect: Opens out rather than closing down; suits a paragraph whose implications widen.

paragraph_rhythm.name: alternating density
paragraph_rhythm.definition: Following a syntactically dense paragraph with an airy one, and vice versa.
paragraph_rhythm.example: A paragraph of subordinated argument followed by three plain declaratives.
paragraph_rhythm.effect: Gives the reader recovery time; sustained density without relief is why difficult books get abandoned.

paragraph_rhythm.name: drop line
paragraph_rhythm.definition: A very short paragraph placed immediately after a long one.
paragraph_rhythm.example: A 200-word paragraph, then: It was already too late.
paragraph_rhythm.effect: Paragraph-scale version of the hammer sentence; the white space above it does the work.

paragraph_rhythm.name: paragraph length contour
paragraph_rhythm.definition: The shape traced by consecutive paragraph lengths across a section.
paragraph_rhythm.example: Long, long, short, long, very short at the section end.
paragraph_rhythm.effect: The rhythm readers perceive before they read a word, because they see the page first.
paragraph_rhythm.caution: Uniform paragraph blocks are visible as monotony from arm's length; check the page as a picture.

paragraph_rhythm.name: coda paragraph
paragraph_rhythm.definition: A short closing paragraph that adds no new information but resolves the section's rhythm.
paragraph_rhythm.example: A single sentence restating the stake in plain monosyllables after an argued section.
paragraph_rhythm.effect: Gives the reader a landing; without one, a section ends where the argument stops rather than where the reader can rest.
paragraph_rhythm.caution: A coda that summarizes rather than resolves is filler — cut it.

paragraph_rhythm.name: hook and turn
paragraph_rhythm.definition: A paragraph that opens with its most arresting sentence and pivots at a mid-paragraph hinge.
paragraph_rhythm.example: An opening claim, three sentences of support, then: Except that none of it held up.
paragraph_rhythm.effect: Keeps the paragraph from being a flat block of support by putting a rhythmic event in its middle.

paragraph_rhythm.name: anaphoric paragraph openings
paragraph_rhythm.definition: Successive paragraphs beginning with the same word or construction.
paragraph_rhythm.example: Three paragraphs in a row opening on: Consider...
paragraph_rhythm.effect: Deliberately used, it structures a section as a series of parallel cases.
paragraph_rhythm.caution: Accidentally used, it is a rut. The commonest unnoticed forms are consecutive paragraphs opening on But, This, or a participial phrase.

paragraph_rhythm.name: white-space rhythm
paragraph_rhythm.definition: The visual pattern of text and gaps on the spread, considered as a rhythmic property of the page.
paragraph_rhythm.example: A spread with one short paragraph, two long ones, and a section break.
paragraph_rhythm.effect: Readers form an impression of difficulty from the page image before reading; managing it is part of managing pace.

paragraph_rhythm.name: block monotony
paragraph_rhythm.definition: Page after page of paragraphs of near-identical length and internal shape.
paragraph_rhythm.example: Every paragraph four to five sentences, every sentence of similar length.
paragraph_rhythm.caution: Quantitatively detectable and a known signature of unedited machine drafting; the fix is structural, not lexical.

paragraph_rhythm.name: breath-unit paragraph
paragraph_rhythm.definition: Sizing a paragraph to the span of attention a reader can spend before wanting a break — in practice, roughly a screen or a third of a page.
paragraph_rhythm.example: Paragraphs of 60 to 120 words in trade nonfiction.
paragraph_rhythm.effect: Matches paragraph length to the reader's endurance rather than to the writer's train of thought.

paragraph_rhythm.name: section rhythm
paragraph_rhythm.definition: Variation in the lengths of the sections or scenes that make up a chapter.
paragraph_rhythm.example: A 1,400-word section, a 300-word one, then an 900-word one.
paragraph_rhythm.effect: The highest level at which pace is felt; a chapter of equal-length sections reads as programmatic even when each section is good.

rhythm_faults.name: accidental meter
rhythm_faults.definition: Prose that falls into a regular metrical pattern, most often iambic pentameter, without intending to.
rhythm_faults.example: The morning light was falling on the stair.
rhythm_faults.effect: Lends unearned solemnity and makes the reader hear verse where prose was meant.
rhythm_faults.caution: Common in writers who read poetry; scan any sentence that sounds unusually good.

rhythm_faults.name: jingle
rhythm_faults.definition: Unintended rhyme between nearby words in prose.
rhythm_faults.example: The reduction in production caused frustration in the nation.
rhythm_faults.effect: Trivializes; the reader hears doggerel and stops attending to the content.
rhythm_faults.caution: Watch -tion, -ing, and -ly endings in particular; they rhyme by default.

rhythm_faults.name: sing-song
rhythm_faults.definition: Regular alternation of stress and equal-length units sustained long enough for the reader to predict the pattern.
rhythm_faults.example: A paragraph of clauses all in trochaic fours.
rhythm_faults.effect: Reads as nursery rhyme regardless of subject.
rhythm_faults.caution: The cure is substitution: break one unit's length or invert one foot.

rhythm_faults.name: tongue-twister
rhythm_faults.definition: A sequence whose articulation is physically difficult because of repeated similar-but-different consonants.
rhythm_faults.effect: The reader trips, rereads, and loses the thread.
rhythm_faults.caution: Invisible on the page and obvious aloud — a read-aloud pass catch.

rhythm_faults.name: echo
rhythm_faults.definition: The same distinctive word or sound reappearing within a few lines without intent.
rhythm_faults.example: The report reported that reporting had improved.
rhythm_faults.effect: Reads as carelessness; the ear flags the repetition before the eye does.
rhythm_faults.caution: Distinguish from deliberate polyptoton — the test is whether the repetition means anything.

rhythm_faults.name: alliterative overload
rhythm_faults.definition: Alliteration sustained past the point where it can pass as accident.
rhythm_faults.example: a bitter, brittle, brooding, backward-looking bureaucracy
rhythm_faults.effect: The prose calls attention to its own cleverness and loses the subject.
rhythm_faults.caution: Two alliterating stresses read as craft; four read as parody.

rhythm_faults.name: stress clash pile-up
rhythm_faults.definition: Several adjacent monosyllabic stresses in sequence, none of them intended for emphasis.
rhythm_faults.example: Ten large black steel drums stood stacked back near that far wall.
rhythm_faults.effect: Every word demands a beat, so none gets one; the sentence sounds like a list read aloud by a machine.

rhythm_faults.name: triad addiction
rhythm_faults.definition: Reflexive resort to three-part structures for every list, clause set, and section.
rhythm_faults.example: Every paragraph ending on three parallel items of increasing length.
rhythm_faults.effect: The pattern becomes the only thing the reader hears.
rhythm_faults.caution: Measurable: count tricolons per thousand words. Machine-drafted prose runs several times the rate of edited human prose, which makes this a first-pass de-slop target.

rhythm_faults.name: dash dependence
rhythm_faults.definition: Using the em dash wherever a comma, colon, period, or parenthesis would serve.
rhythm_faults.example: Three dashes in a single paragraph, none marking a genuine swerve.
rhythm_faults.effect: Every interruption stops feeling like an interruption; the sentence's shape flattens.
rhythm_faults.caution: Quantitatively tracked as an AI tell. Replace two-thirds of them and see which the sentence actually misses.

rhythm_faults.name: fragment addiction
rhythm_faults.definition: Sentence fragments used so often that they become the default rhythm.
rhythm_faults.example: Not because it worked. Because it was cheap. Because no one asked.
rhythm_faults.effect: Urgency inflation; the reader habituates and the fragments read as mannerism.
rhythm_faults.caution: Fragments derive their force entirely from contrast with complete syntax.

rhythm_faults.name: metronomic clause length
rhythm_faults.definition: Clauses within sentences all landing at the same length, even when sentence lengths vary.
rhythm_faults.example: Every sentence a pair of eight-word clauses joined by a comma.
rhythm_faults.effect: Variance measured at the sentence level looks fine while the prose still sounds mechanical.
rhythm_faults.caution: Sentence-length variance alone will not catch this; scan clause boundaries too.

rhythm_faults.name: trailing-off close
rhythm_faults.definition: A sentence or paragraph that ends on unstressed, low-content material after its real point has passed.
rhythm_faults.example: ...which is something that should be taken into consideration going forward.
rhythm_faults.effect: Discards the strongest position in the sentence.
rhythm_faults.caution: The commonest fixable cadence fault in draft prose. Find the last content word that matters and end there.

rhythm_faults.name: rhythmic tic
rhythm_faults.definition: An unconscious signature cadence — a favored clause shape, opener, or close — repeated across a whole manuscript.
rhythm_faults.example: Every third sentence built as short clause, comma, long clause, comma, three-word tag.
rhythm_faults.effect: Invisible to the writer, unmistakable to a reader who finishes the book.
rhythm_faults.caution: Only detectable by measurement or a fresh reader; it is what a construction-variety report is for.
